kf1.tip: Sketch from memory a cross-section of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge under Iceland, labelling the two plates, rising magma, new crust and runny basalt lava.
kf1.note: A good sketch shows two plates with arrows pointing away from each other and a gap between them at the ridge. Magma rises up through that gap. Label where it cools to form new crust on either side. Show runny basalt lava flowing steadily out rather than exploding, with Iceland sitting on top of the ridge. If your arrows point towards each other, you have drawn a destructive margin instead.

kf2.tip: Argue for and against this claim: living by the San Andreas Fault is safer than living by a destructive margin because there are no volcanoes. Then decide.
kf2.note: A strong answer weighs three things. The San Andreas Fault has no volcanoes because no plate is being subducted. But friction locks the plates until they jolt free, so the earthquake risk is severe. A destructive margin brings both massive earthquakes and explosive eruptions. Most would decide it faces fewer types of hazard, but 'safer' overstates it. If you treated no volcanoes as meaning safe, you ignored how powerful the earthquakes there are.

cs1.tip: Write the chain of steps from a subducting oceanic plate to Mount St Helens in 1980. Circle the one link that makes the eruption explosive instead of gentle.
cs1.note: A strong chain runs like this. The denser oceanic plate is forced down, carrying water and trapped gas. Heat melts it in the mantle. The water and gas mix with the magma, which is forced upwards under enormous pressure. The gas escapes violently, blowing out the side of Mount St Helens. Most would circle the water and gas mixing into the magma. If you circled the melting, remember magma at constructive margins erupts gently.
